flawed_step: The claim that a vertex's distance is final when it is extracted fails once negative edges exist. A later negative edge can create a shorter path to a vertex that is already settled, and to vertices that were reached through it.
counterexample: Digraph with edges s->a (2), s->b (4), b->a (-3), a->c (1). It has no cycles, so no negative cycle. True distances: a=1 (s-b-a), b=4, c=2 (s-b-a-c). Dijkstra trace: extract s(0), which sets a=2 and b=4; extract a(2), which is final and sets c=3; extract c(3), which is final; extract b(4), where relaxing b->a would give 1 but a is settled, and c is never re-relaxed. Reported dist(c)=3, true dist(c)=2 (and reported dist(a)=2, true 1).
assessment_summary: The statement is false. A 4-vertex graph with no cycles and one negative edge makes label-setting Dijkstra settle a and c too early. It reports c=3 when the true distance is 2. This holds even if the algorithm overwrites the label of an already-settled vertex, because c is never relaxed again.
